title: Adding and Subtracting Unlike Fractions in Grade 5 (LCD Made Simple) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Adding and Subtracting Unlike Fractions: Grade 5
meta_desc: Learn adding and subtracting unlike fractions in Grade 5: find the LCD, make equivalent fractions, then add or subtract. Free quiz and printable worksheet.
excerpt: A Grade 5 child can already add halves and quarters when the denominators match. The moment they differ, everything stalls. Here is the LCD method I use to fix that, step by step, with a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Adding and subtracting unlike fractions is the exact point in Grade 5 where confident children suddenly freeze. Ask them for 1/4 + 2/4 and the hand shoots up: three-quarters, easy. Change it to 1/4 + 1/3 and you get a guess — usually 2/7, because they add the tops and the bottoms. That single mistake, adding denominator to denominator, is the thing this whole lesson exists to fix.

The rule is short: you can only add or subtract fractions when their denominators are the same. Quarters add to quarters, thirds to thirds. When the denominators differ, they are unlike fractions, and the job is to rewrite them so they share one common denominator first. Everything below is about doing that cleanly.

Why unlike denominators cannot be added directly

Denominators are not just numbers; they are the size of the piece. A quarter of a roti and a third of a roti are different-sized pieces, so you cannot count them together any more than you can add 3 apples and 2 mangoes and call it 5 apples. First you make the pieces the same size. That shared size is the common denominator, and the smallest one that works is the lowest common denominator (LCD) — which is just the LCM of the two denominators.

The three-step method for adding and subtracting unlike fractions

I teach it as the same three steps every single time, whether the sign is plus or minus. Grade 5 children do far better with one reliable routine than with clever shortcuts.

  • Step 1 — Find the LCD. Take the LCM of the two denominators. For 1/4 and 1/3 the LCM of 4 and 3 is 12.
  • Step 2 — Make equivalent fractions. Multiply the top and bottom of each fraction by whatever turns its denominator into the LCD. 1/4 = 3/12 (times 3), and 1/3 = 4/12 (times 4).
  • Step 3 — Add or subtract the numerators. Keep the common denominator, combine only the tops: 3/12 + 4/12 = 7/12. Then simplify if you can.

So 1/4 + 1/3 = 7/12, not 2/7. Subtraction is identical: 1/3 − 1/4 = 4/12 − 3/12 = 1/12.

Finding the LCD without guessing

Two tricks cover almost every Grade 5 case. If one denominator divides the other — like 3 and 6 — the bigger one is the LCD, so 6 is your common denominator and you only need to change the 3. If the denominators share no common factor — like 4 and 5, or 2 and 3 — just multiply them: the LCD is 20, or 6. The tricky middle case, such as 6 and 8, is where you list multiples (6, 12, 18, 24… and 8, 16, 24…) and grab the first match: 24.

Notice the third row: 6 and 4 do not multiply to their LCD (that would be 24 and would still work, just with bigger numbers). The LCD is 12. Using a bigger common denominator is not wrong — the answer simplifies to the same thing — but the LCD keeps the arithmetic small, which matters when a ten-year-old is doing it by hand.

Mixed numbers: the Grade 5 extension

Once plain unlike fractions are secure, mixed numbers are the natural next step, and they turn up all over Grade 5 word problems. There are two honest routes. The one I prefer for beginners: convert each mixed number to an improper fraction first, then run the same three steps.

Take 2 1/2 + 1 1/3. Convert: 2 1/2 = 5/2 and 1 1/3 = 4/3. LCD of 2 and 3 is 6, so 5/2 = 15/6 and 4/3 = 8/6. Add the tops: 15/6 + 8/6 = 23/6, which is 3 5/6. No borrowing, no separate whole-number column to forget about. The alternative — adding whole numbers and fractions separately — is faster once fluent but causes regrouping errors early on, so I hold it back until the improper-fraction method is automatic.

The one caveat worth stating

Always simplify the final answer, but simplify last, not midway. I have watched children reduce 3/12 to 1/4 in the middle of a subtraction and then lose the common denominator entirely. Combine first, tidy up at the end.

A quick classroom check

  • Denominators same? — add or subtract straight away.
  • Denominators different? — find the LCD, rewrite, then combine the numerators.
  • Only ever touch the tops once the bottoms match.
  • Mixed numbers? — make them improper first.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The eight questions below cover exactly this — finding the LCD, making equivalent fractions, and adding and subtracting unlike fractions, including a couple of mixed numbers. Let your child work each one on paper before picking an answer, then read the explanations for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer graded practice, the printable Grade 5 worksheet at the end has plenty more, each with a full answer key.

quiz.about: Grade 5 adding and subtracting unlike fractions

questions.q: What is the lowest common denominator of 1/4 and 1/3?
questions.explanation: The LCD is the LCM of 4 and 3. Since 4 and 3 share no common factor, multiply them: 4 x 3 = 12.
LCD of 2 and 3 is 6. Rewrite as 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

questions.q: Rewrite 2/3 with a denominator of 15. What is the numerator?
questions.explanation: To turn 3 into 15 you multiply by 5, so multiply the top by 5 too: 2 x 5 = 10, giving 10/15.
LCD of 6 and 4 is 12. Rewrite as 10/12 - 3/12 = 7/12.

questions.q: Why can you not just add 1/4 + 1/3 to get 2/7?
options: The pieces are different sizes until the denominators match
You must add the numerators to the denominators
questions.explanation: Unlike fractions have different-sized pieces. You must make a common denominator first, then add only the numerators: 3/12 + 4/12 = 7/12.

questions.q: What is 2 1/2 + 1 1/3 as a mixed number?

questions.explanation: Since 4 divides 8, the LCD is 8. Rewrite 1/4 as 2/8, then 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8.

faq.q: What does adding and subtracting unlike fractions mean in Grade 5?
faq.a: Unlike fractions have different denominators, such as 1/4 and 1/3. To add or subtract them you first rewrite both with a common denominator — the LCD — then combine only the numerators.

faq.q: How do you find the lowest common denominator?
faq.a: Take the LCM of the two denominators. If one divides the other, the bigger one is the LCD. If they share no factor, multiply them. Otherwise list multiples of each and pick the first that matches.
Because you never add denominators. Quarters and thirds are different-sized pieces, so you first make them the same size — 3/12 and 4/12 — then add the tops to get 7/12.

faq.q: How do you add mixed numbers with unlike fractions?
faq.a: The simplest reliable way is to convert each mixed number to an improper fraction, find the LCD, add or subtract the numerators, then change the result back to a mixed number and simplify.
